'Not hungry.'
'You got the physics paper back today, na?'
'Eleven out of forty.'

'You feel useless. That's real. But feelings aren't report cards.' Chaitanya waited. 'Come and eat. Tomorrow we'll look at which questions went wrong.'
Slowly, the pillow came down.

passage: I'm Lalit, and in Class 10 I failed the first maths unit test, 9 out of 40. What I remember most isn't the mark. It's the weight afterwards, like wet sand in my chest. I walked home thinking: I feel worthless, so I am worthless. It seemed obvious. Feelings don't lie, right? That week I stopped going to cricket and stopped answering my cousin Pradeep's messages. Then Pradeep turned up at our door with two samosas and said, 'You failed a test. You didn't fail at being a person.' I argued. But I remember going quiet, because part of me knew the feeling had shouted louder than the facts. I still get that wet-sand feeling sometimes. Now I try to say, 'That's the mood talking,' before I believe it.

Counsellor's note, Tuesday, Class 9
Naveen's class teacher sent him to me after he tore up his chemistry test (14/50) in class. He sat with his hood up and said very little at first. Then: 'I feel like rubbish, so obviously I am rubbish.' He said it as if reading a fact off the board. I asked what else he had done this term. After a long pause: the science model that won second place, and teaching his little sister to ride a cycle. He didn't want those to count. I told him the heavy feeling after a bad mark is real and worth listening to, but it is a mood, not a measurement of him. We planned to see the chemistry teacher together on Thursday. I have called his mother about today and asked her to check in with him tonight. I will see him again on Friday.
Suraj, school counsellor

Tuesday night

Chemistry test back: 14 out of 50. Kamal got 41 and he didn't even revise.

I haven't eaten dinner. I feel so heavy, like someone poured cement into me. And I keep thinking: I feel useless, so I must be useless. It's not a thought. It's just true. You can't feel this bad about yourself unless it's right.

I wrote "stupid" in pencil on the back of the test, then rubbed it out, then wrote it again.

Papa knocked at ten. I said I was sleeping. He came in anyway and sat on the floor by the bed. He didn't ask about marks. He said, "Beti, you look like the day your cycle got stolen." I told him the number. He said, "That's one test on one Tuesday. It's not the whole Arohi." Then he said we'd go through it together on Saturday and ask ma'am which topics to redo.

I still feel heavy. But I ate the toast he brought.

— Arohi

qa.a: Kamal might feel awkward or sorry, since he didn't mean his mark to be a comparison. He might also want to help her revise.
